body.p: Claims 1, 2, 8, 9, 15, and 16 have been amended herein. Upon the entry of the amendments, Claims 1-22 remain pending in this application. The amendments to Claims 1, 8, and 15 are supported, for example, by [ 0038], [0051], and [0062] and FIG. 2B of the originally filed specification, hereinafter "Specification." The amendments to Claims 2, 9, and 16 are supported, for example, by 1 [0051]-[0053] and FIG. 2B of the Specification. As such, the claim amendments do not introduce new matter. Entry of the amendments is respectfully requested.

Applicant respectfully traverses the rejections, the characterizations of the pending claims, and any implicit and/or explicit reliance on Official Notice. Applicant respectfully requests reconsideration of the application in view of the above amendment and remarks set forth below.
Discussion of Rejection of Claims under 35 U.S.C. @ 103

Claims 1-3, 7-10, 14-17, and 20-22 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 103 as being unpatentable over Takeuchi et al. (U.S. Patent Pub. No. 2017/0259433, hereinafter "Takeuchi") in view of Takenaka et al. (U.S. Patent Pub. No. 2005/0104548, hereinafter "Takenaka") and Diolaiti et al. (U.S. Patent Pub. No. 2011/0202068, hereinafter "Diolaiti").

Claims 4-6, 11-13, 18, and 19 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 103 as being unpatentable over Takeuchi in view of Takenaka and Diolaiti and further in view of Nakasu et al. (U.S. Patent Pub. No. 2020/0306965, hereinafter "Nakasu").
Standard for 35 U.S.C. @ 103

The Patent and Trademark Office has the burden under 35 U.S.C. § 103 to establish a prima facie case of obviousness. The rationale to support a conclusion that the claim would have been obvious is that all the claimed elements were known in the prior art and one skilled in the art could have combined the elements as claimed by known methods with no change in their respective functions, and the combination yielded nothing more than predictable results to one of ordinary skill in the art. It can be important to identify a reason that would have prompted a person of ordinary skill in the relevant field to combine the elements in the way the claimed new invention does. If any of these findings cannot be made, then this rationale cannot be used to support a conclusion that the claim would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art. M.P.E.P. § 2143.

Applicant respectfully submits that the cited references do not teach the combination of elements recited in each of independent Claims 1, 8, and 15, as amended. For example, with respect to Claim 1, the cited references do not teach or suggest at least the claimed method comprising "assigning a first impedance value to the end effector along the at least one axis of freedom of the constrained object and assigning a second impedance value to the end effector along the at least one constrained axis of the constrained object, the second impedance value indicating a greater amount of impedance than the first impedance value." Amended independent Claims 8 and 15 include similar features.

In rejecting previously pending Claim 1, the Examiner relies on Diolaiti as allegedly teaching "assigning a first impedance value to the end effector along the at least one axis of freedom of the constrained object and assigning a second impedance value to the end effector along the at least one constrained axis of the constrained object." Office Action, page 5 (citing Diolaiti, FIG. 10 and [0071]).

Diolaiti states that "the Surgeon may also specify the weighting for each of the state variables used for calculating the setpoint in equation (1) using the stiffness selector block 1052.... Thus, separate weights may be defined by the Surgeon for each state variable so as to suit the Surgeon's personal preferences." Diolaiti, [0071]. Diolaiti further states that a "setpoint generator block 1050 receives the commanded state vector (XDES) for the camera instrument 211 in the output 1021 of the scale and offset processing block 1001, a preferred pose vector (Xpp) for the camera instrument 211 in an output 1055 of a pose selector block 1051, and weightings (wi, i=1 ... n) for the state variables of the commanded state vector (XDES), and calculates a setpoint vector (Xsp) for its output 1057 by interpolating between the commanded state vector (XDES) and the preferred pose vector (Xpp) using the weightings (wi, i=1 ... n) in a weighted average approach." Id., [0065].
Diolaiti described the effect of this process as follows:

the weightings (wi, i=1 ... n) applied by the setpoint generator 1050 also serve to determine the magnitudes of the force feedback in each of the translational and orientational directions in the form of forces and torques felt by the Surgeon on the input device 108. Thus, heavier weighted state variables that refer to translational movement of the input device 108 and camera 211 result in higher force feedback gains felt on the input device 108 as resisting translational movement away from the preferred pose (Xpp) and heavier weighted
state variables that refer to orientational movement of the input device 108 and camera 211 result in higher torque feedback gains felt on the input device 108 as resisting orientational movement
away from the preferred pose (Xpp).

Based on the above, Applicant respectfully submits that Diolaiti at best relates to allowing a surgeon to specify the weighting for each state variable used for calculating a setpoint using the stiffness selector block. These weighting are used by the setpoint generator block 1050 to weight the state variables of the commanded state vector (XDES), providing force feedback to an input device 108 to resist movement away from a preferred pose (Xpp).

However, Applicant respectfully submits that specifying weighting for state variables used in calculating resistance for deviating from a preferred pose is not the same as setting impedance values along the axis of freedom or constrained axis of a constrained object. Thus, Diolaiti does not teach or suggest setting a first impedance value along an axis of freedom of a constrained object and a second impedance value along a constrained axis of the constrained object, where the second impedance value indicates a greater amount of impedance than the first impedance value.

In addition, Diolaiti states that "the instrument may have internal mechanical constraints (e.g., cables, gearing, cams and belts, etc.) that force multiple joints to move together in a pre- determined fashion. Each set of mechanically constrained joints implements a specific axis of motion, and constraints may be devised to pair rotational joints (e.g., joggle joints)." Diolaiti, [ 0039]. Thus, Diolaiti at best contemplates mechanical constraints that are internal to the instrument but does not relate to an axis of freedom or a constrained axis of another object.

Since Diolaiti does not teach or suggest determining an axis of freedom or a constrained axis of a constrained object, Applicant respectfully submits that Diolaiti does not teach or suggest assigning the weighting for each state variable used for calculating a setpoint to any axis associated with a constrained object.

For at least the above reasons, Applicant respectfully submits that Diolaiti fails to teach or suggest the feature "assigning a first impedance value to the end effector along the at least one axis of freedom of the constrained object and assigning a second impedance value to the end effector along the at least one constrained axis of the constrained object" of amended Claim 1.
The other references were cited merely to supposedly show certain features which are unrelated to the above-indicated feature and these references do not remedy the deficiencies of

Diolaiti. Therefore, the combination of the cited references does not teach or suggest all of the features of each of independent Claims 1, 8, and 15. Thus, not all claim elements were known in the cited references. Furthermore, the Examiner did not identify a reason, at least with respect to the above-identified feature, that would have prompted a person of ordinary skill in the relevant field to combine the elements in the way the claimed invention does. In view of the above, Applicant respectfully submits that no prima facie case of obviousness has been established with respect to Claims 1, 8, and 15 and thus, these claims are patentable over the cited references.

Claims 2-7, 9-14, and 16-21 depend from one of base Claims 1, 8, and 15, and further define additional technical features. In view of the patentability of their base claim, and in further view of the additional technical features, Applicant respectfully submits that the dependent claims are patentable over the cited references. Furthermore, Applicant does not necessarily agree with the characterization of the cited references made by the Examiner in rejecting the dependent claims.

Although the present communication may include alterations to the application or claims, or characterizations of claim scope or referenced art, Applicant is not conceding in this application that previously pending claims are not patentable over the cited references. Rather, any alterations or characterizations are being made to facilitate expeditious prosecution of this application. Applicant reserves the right to pursue at a later date any previously pending or other broader or narrower claims that capture any subject matter supported by the present disclosure, including subject matter found to be specifically disclaimed herein or by any prior prosecution. Accordingly, reviewers of this or any parent, child or related prosecution history shall not reasonably infer that Applicant has made any disclaimers or disavowals of any subject matter supported by the present application.

Applicant has endeavored to address all of the Examiner's concerns as expressed in the outstanding Office Action. Reconsideration and withdrawal of the outstanding rejections is respectfully requested.
